files.lesson.md: --- order: 7 unit: circles node: AC9M7M03 n2 uses: [AC9M7N06 n2] # dividing decimals title: Discovering π summary: "Roll any circle out flat and its circumference is just over 3 of its diameters. C ÷ d is the same number for every circle: π (pi), about 3.14. π's digits never end: 3.14 and 22/7 are close, not exact." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A bike wheel, a coin and the Earth's equator: wildly different sizes, but for each one the distance round is the same number of times the distance across." connection: wheel-roll app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8279 url: http://127.0.0.1:8279/index.html readySelector: ".gbar button" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: circle.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Rolled out flat, the circumference is 3 diameters and a little bit more (about 0.14 of a diameter): $C \\div d \\approx 3.14$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@circle.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Roll it out" say: "Roll the circle out flat." clip: - caption: { text: "Mark a point and roll the circle one full turn.", say: "Mark a point and roll the circle one full turn." } - click: Roll it out - wait: 2800 - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "circumference 9.42" } - caption: { text: "The track is 3 diameters and a bit: C ÷ d ≈ 3.14.", say: "The track is three diameters and a little bit more." } - wait: 1600 --- The **circumference** of a circle is hard to measure with a ruler, because it is curved. But you can roll the circle along a line for one full turn: the track it leaves is exactly its circumference, laid flat. ## Predict: diameter 10 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to an estimate for the circumference of a 10 cm circle shows whether they expect a fixed multiple of the diameter, and roughly what it is." check: type: predict q: "A circle has diameter 10 cm. Roughly how long is its circumference?" options: ["About 31 cm", "About 20 cm", "About 10 cm", "About 100 cm"] actual: "About 31 cm: just over 3 diameters (31.4 cm). 20 cm would be 2 diameters, which is less than the way round." ``` Picture walking round a circle compared with walking across it. ## Run: roll three circles ```step stage: run insight: "Rolling circles of three sizes and dividing C by d each time shows the ratio is the same, about 3.14, whatever the size." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Roll out at least three circles of different sizes. Look at C ÷ d in the table. Was your prediction right?", when: "n >= 3", explain: "C ÷ d is 3.14 every time: the circumference is π diameters." } ``` Change the radius, then press **Roll it out**. Each size adds a row to the table. Here's what the three circles showed. Compare that track with the **diameter**, and something remarkable happens: for every circle, big or small, the circumference is the same number of diameters. That number is called **π** (the Greek letter pi, said "pie"): $$\pi = \frac{C}{d} \approx 3.14$$ People have known this for a long time: an Egyptian text, the Rhind papyrus, written about 1650 BC, already uses a value close to 3.16 ([MacTutor History of Mathematics](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Pi_through_the_ages/)). ## Investigate: the same number every time ```step stage: investigate insight: "C ÷ d is the same for every circle; Kai's measurement gives 3.14, but π is not exactly 3.14. A quick estimate uses C ≈ 3d." tasks: - check: type: question q: "What does the table show about C ÷ d?" options: ["It is about 3.14 for every circle", "It gets bigger for bigger circles", "It is 2, because the diameter is two radii", "It changes every time"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "C and d both get bigger, but their ratio stays the same.", "That is d ÷ r, not C ÷ d.", "Look again at the last column."] explain: "C ÷ d is the same number for every circle: π ≈ 3.14." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kai" text: "Kai measures a plate to find π. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: pi-exact explain: "Line 3: a measurement gives π only to a few places. π = 3.14159… has digits that never end or settle into a pattern; 3.14 is an approximation." - check: type: number q: "A wheel has diameter 60 cm. Estimate its circumference in cm, using π ≈ 3.14." answer: 188.4 tolerance: 0.5 explain: "C ≈ 3.14 × 60 = 188.4 cm (quick check: 3 × 60 = 180, a bit more)." ``` ### What π means Here is what π is, and what it is not. ```worked \pi = C \div d :: π is how many diameters fit round the circumference. \pi = 3.14159265\ldots :: Its digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern. \pi \approx 3.14 \quad \text{or} \quad \pi \approx \tfrac{22}{7} :: Two handy approximations (22/7 = 3.142…). C \approx 3 \times d :: A quick estimate: a bit more than 3 diameters. ``` Now: what does the table show? ### Find the mistake Read Kai's reasoning. Is a measurement ever exact? ### Estimate ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a circle of diameter 1 (so C is π itself), π from a measurement, a quick estimate, and the edge case of a bigger circle having a bigger π." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#unit", height: 640 } tasks: - starter: "circle.yml#unit" hint: "Diameter 1 means radius 0.5." check: { type: board, text: "Roll out a circle with diameter 1 cm. How long is its circumference?", when: "d = 1 and o = 1", explain: "3.14 cm: a circle 1 across is π round." } - check: type: answer q: "A bin lid measures circumference 47.1 cm and diameter 15 cm. What is C ÷ d?" answer: "3.14" feedback: - ["32.1", "That subtracts. Divide."] explain: "47.1 ÷ 15 = 3.14." - check: type: question q: "A round pond is 2 m across. About how far is it round?" options: ["About 6.3 m", "About 4 m", "About 2 m", "About 12 m"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is 2 diameters. Round is just over 3.", "That is the diameter.", "That uses 6 diameters."] explain: "C ≈ 3.14 × 2 = 6.28 m." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: is π bigger for a bigger circle?" options: ["No: π is the same for every circle", "Yes: a bigger circle has a longer circumference", "Only for circles over 1 m"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "C is bigger, but so is d, by the same factor.", "Every circle gives the same C ÷ d."] explain: "Double the diameter and the circumference doubles too, so C ÷ d stays π." ``` ### Diameter 1 Each task changes one thing. ### π from a measurement ### A quick estimate ### Bigger circles ## Practise: π ```step stage: practise insight: "Estimating and working out circumferences and the meaning of π, mixed; π as exact is the planted slip; the review keeps radius and diameter fresh." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Using π ≈ 22/7, about how long is the circumference of a circle with diameter 7 cm?" options: ["22 cm", "14 cm", "7 cm", "49 cm"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is 2 diameters.", "That is the diameter.", "That is 7 × 7."] explain: "22/7 × 7 = 22 cm." - check: type: number q: "A circle has circumference 31.4 cm. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is its diameter, in cm?" answer: 10 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "C ÷ π = d: 31.4 ÷ 3.14 = 10 cm." - check: type: question q: "Which is true?" options: ["π is a little more than 3.14", "π is exactly 3.14", "π is exactly 22/7", "π is 3"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "3.14 is π rounded.", "22/7 = 3.1428…, a little more than π.", "3 is a rough estimate."] explain: "π = 3.14159…: a little more than 3.14, a little less than 22/7." - check: type: answer q: "Review: a circle has diameter 14 cm. What is its radius, in cm?" answer: "7" feedback: - ["28", "That doubles."] explain: "14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm." ``` ### 22/7 ### Backwards: the diameter ### What π is ### Review: radius ## Make: a circumference between 12 and 13 ```step stage: make insight: "Searching for a circle with a circumference in a given range uses C ≈ 3.14d backwards as a prediction, checked by rolling." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#unit", height: 640 } hint: ["12 ÷ 3.14 is about 4. What radius gives diameter 4?", "Predict first, then roll to check."] check: { type: board, text: "Find and roll out a circle whose circumference is between 12 cm and 13 cm.", when: "c > 12 and c < 13 and o = 1", explain: "Diameter 4 cm (radius 2): C = π × 4 ≈ 12.57 cm (3.14 × 4 = 12.56)." } ``` Predict the diameter before you roll. ## Make: roll a wheel, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Rolling a wheel one turn gives C, and the width across gives d; the lengths come in different units, so changing to one unit comes before dividing." hint: ["Write both lengths in centimetres.", "C ÷ d: the way round divided by the way across."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A bike wheel is rolled one full turn along the floor. It goes 2.2 m. The wheel is 70 cm across. Work out C ÷ d, to two decimal places." steps: - ["Same unit: $2.2$ m $= 220$ cm", "C and d must be in the same unit before dividing"] - ["$C \\div d = 220 \\div 70$", "the way round divided by the way across"] - ["$\\approx 3.14$", "close to π, as for every circle"] picks: - step: 1 q: "Why change 2.2 m to 220 cm first?" options: - "C and d must be in the same unit before you divide" - "Centimetres make the answer bigger" - "Metres cannot be divided by centimetres" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The unit should not change the answer. A ratio of two lengths in the same unit has none.", "You can divide them, but the answer means nothing until both are in one unit."] answer: "3.14" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["0.03", "That divides metres by centimetres. Change both to one unit first."] - ["0.32", "That is d ÷ C, upside down. Divide the way round by the way across."] criteria: - "I changed both lengths to the same unit." - "I divided the circumference by the diameter, not the other way round." - "I compared my answer with 3.14 and said why it might be a little off." explain: "220 ÷ 70 ≈ 3.14, so the way round is just over 3 diameters, as for every circle." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The distance is made up for the task, and a real wheel gives a similar number, a little off because the tyre squashes. Change the unit, divide, compare with 3.14, and type the ratio. **Also used in** - **Cycling.** A bike computer needs the wheel's circumference, which is π times the wheel's width across. - **Racing.** In a 400 m race the outer lanes start further forward, because each lane's bends make a bigger circle. - **Round things in the room.** A tin, a plate and a coin all give about the same C ÷ d. ```teacher summary: Students roll circles of different sizes out flat, divide the circumference by the diameter each time, and discover the constant π ≈ 3.14, with its approximations and a quick estimate C ≈ 3d (AC9M7M03, node 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - "I can explain what π means: how many diameters fit round a circle." - I can estimate a circumference from a diameter. - I can say why 3.14 and 22/7 are close to π but not exact. struggle: Believing the ratio is the same for every circle before seeing it. Ask students to predict C ÷ d for a much bigger circle before they roll it, and let the table decide. before: > Do the Run board yourself first, then try it with real objects: string round tins and plates, measured against their diameters. The board is the clean version; the hands-on measurement shows why measured values wobble around 3.14. The one idea: C ÷ d is the same for every circle, and that number is π. The common mistake is thinking π is exactly 3.14 or 22/7 (Kai's mistake). running: - "Predict: take estimates; most say 20 or 30." - "Run: ask students to read down the C ÷ d column aloud." - "Investigate: collect real measurements from tins and plates; their ratios cluster near 3.1 or 3.2." - "Modify: diameter 1 gives π itself: link to the definition." - "Make: insist on a prediction before rolling." - "Paper: the rolled wheel is worked in books; the page marks C ÷ d and the reason for one unit, then shows a model. Books out, and look for 220 cm written before the divide." stuck: - see: A student thinks π is exactly 3.14 (Kai's mistake). ask: Is any ruler measurement exact? fix: π = 3.14159… never ends; 3.14 is rounded. - see: A student divides d by C. ask: "How many diameters fit round: is the answer more or less than 1?" fix: C ÷ d, about 3. - see: A student thinks bigger circles have bigger π. ask: If the diameter doubles, what happens to the circumference? fix: Both double, so the ratio stays the same. stretch: Find out how Archimedes trapped π between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 using polygons inside and outside a circle. support: Use string and tins; keep the table of C, d and C ÷ d on the board. leads: > Next: Circumference (node 3): C = πd and C = 2πr, and finding d from C. Where it leads: the area of a circle (Year 8), and π as an irrational number (Year 9). exit: q: What is π? Estimate the circumference of a circle with diameter 20 cm. a: π is the circumference divided by the diameter, the same for every circle, about 3.14. C ≈ 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm. explain: > Roll a circle out flat for one turn and its circumference is a bit more than 3 diameters. For **every** circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is the same number, **π**: $$\pi = \frac{C}{d} = 3.14159\ldots$$ π's digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern; 3.14 and $\tfrac{22}{7}$ are approximations. A quick estimate: the circumference is a bit more than 3 diameters. ```
